item.title: Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception
item.guid: title:zooming without zooming v2 from seeing details to connecting evidence for generalizable multimodal perception
item.description: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence.

item.title: LearnPrunerV2: Learnable Progressive Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models
item.guid: title:learnprunerv2 learnable progressive token pruning for vision language models
item.description: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable multimodal capabilities but suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to the massive number of visual tokens. While token pruning is a promising solution, existing methods still suffer from two major drawbacks: 1) unreliable pruning criteria that fail to accurately localize task-specific regions due to inherent attention biases or query-agnostic designs, and 2) suboptimal pruning strategies that employ rigid, non-adaptive schedules, overlooking the dynamic evolution of token redundancy across different model depths. To address these challenges, we propose LearnPrunerV2, which extends the previous two-stage heuristic framework (LearnPruner) into a fully learnable architecture. Specifically, we integrate lightweight learnable modules into every layer of the VLM backbone, which estimate token importance by fusing intrinsic visual saliency with extrinsic query relevance captured via a shadow token. By uncovering a consistent staircase redundancy pattern across VLM layers, we further introduce Budget-Deterministic Pruning (BDP) to establish a hardware-friendly schedule with fixed per-layer budgets. Extensive experimental results across various benchmarks and VLMs demonstrate that LearnPrunerV2 consistently outperform previous state-of-the-art methods.

item.title: When All Rollouts Fail: Policy-Compatible Joint Decoding for Hard-Problem Reasoning
item.guid: title:when all rollouts fail policy compatible joint decoding for hard problem reasoning
item.description: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) derives its learning signal from binary rewards via on-policy exploration and becomes a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning of large language models. Yet it faces a learning cliff on problems beyond model's current ability: when every rollout fails, the samples reveal nothing about a correct solution, and group-relative estimators (e. g. , GRPO, RLOO) collapse the update to zero advantage. Expert trajectories offer a remedy, but they are incompatible with the current policy and often lie in the student's low-probability regions, so the surviving updates demand large parameter shifts and decay into surface-level imitation rather than transferable reasoning. We argue that a useful learning signal on hard problems must be both verifiably correct and sufficiently compatible with the current policy.

item.title: Understanding the limits of latent world models
item.guid: title:understanding the limits of latent world models
item.description: World models are widely proposed as core components for enabling agents to reason over long temporal and spatial horizons. Yet current evaluations often emphasize task performance while providing limited insight into whether learned world models acquire predictive latent dynamics that reflect the underlying structure of the environment. Here we introduce the concept of faithful latent world models as an equivariance condition between the environment's transition map and the learned latent dynamics. We propose latent rollout consistency (LRC) as a metric to evaluate action-conditioned latent prediction. Strikingly, we find that across the studied state of the art latent world models, none solves the task by actually faithfully modeling the dynamics of the environment.

item.title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis
item.guid: title:ontology guided multi agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis
item.description: Effective differential diagnosis depends on well structured and unambiguous patient case descriptions, since incomplete or ambiguous clinical information readily leads to diagnostic errors and inconsistent reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence, and can generate plausible yet unsupported diagnostic conclusions. Their reasoning remains largely opaque, making it difficult for clinicians to assess the evidence and rationale behind a given recommendation. To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multiagent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. The framework grounds diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base, enabling interpretation of symptoms, clinical findings, or disease relationships, while decomposing diagnosis into explicit, auditable reasoning steps. This ontology-based grounding constrains inference to evidence-backed associations, reducing hallucination and improving diagnostic transparency, traceability, and consistency.

item.title: RobotAgentBench: Towards Open-world Robot Autonomy
item.guid: title:robotagentbench towards open world robot autonomy
item.description: Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) have significantly improved robotic manipulation, yet deploying robots in the open world demands a higher level of autonomy beyond executing predefined tasks. Robot agents offer a promising paradigm for this transition, integrating task discovery, contextual reasoning, physical execution, and adaptive recovery into a closed interaction loop. However, existing benchmarks largely evaluate isolated capabilities, failing to capture the complexity of open-world robot autonomy. We introduce RobotAgentBench (RAB), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating robot agents in realistic, open-world household environments. Through an agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline, RAB constructs 50 diverse household layouts with interactive objects and physically grounded tasks, encompassing 90 atomic tasks, 18 short-horizon tasks, 8 long-horizon tasks, and 4 open-ended scenarios. RAB provides a multi-level evaluation of robot agent capabilities: (1) task-level assessments systematically examine five complementary dimensions: task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and robustness; (2) scenario-level evaluation assesses how agents integrate these capabilities to autonomously fulfill high-level user needs.

item.title: VGIQA: Fine-Grained Image Quality Assessment with Visual Grounding Rewards
item.guid: title:vgiqa fine grained image quality assessment with visual grounding rewards
item.description: Image quality assessment (IQA) aims to evaluate the perceptual visual quality of images. Recently, the rapid development of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has significantly advanced the IQA field. By integrating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and reinforcement learning (RL), these models can generate more accurate and interpretable results while relying on less training data. However, existing MLLM-based methods are predominantly constrained to holistic, image-level evaluations and lack the capability to produce fine-grained, localized assessments, which substantially limits their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose VGIQA, a novel IQA model endowed with both local and global quality assessment capabilities. VGIQA is trained via a two-stage paradigm comprising a cold-start phase followed by reinforcement learning.

item.title: MedVTok: A General-Purpose Medical Visual Tokenizer
item.guid: title:medvtok a general purpose medical visual tokenizer
item.description: Multimodal medical AI requires a common visual interface for encoding heterogeneous imaging evidence for patient condition modeling. However, existing medical visual tokenizers are often tied to a specific dimension and imaging modality, forcing multimodal systems to rely on fragmented and poorly reusable representations. We introduce MedVTok, a general-purpose visual tokenizer that maps 2D images and 3D volumes from diverse imaging modalities into a unified token space. Building such a tokenizer poses two key challenges: preserving anatomical structure across dimensions and capturing clinical semantics across modalities. To this end, MedVTok introduces (i) slice differential regularization, which explicitly models inter-slice anatomical coherence missing in previous per-pixel/per-voxel supervision, and (ii) multi-expert representation alignment, which integrates knowledge from multiple medical expert encoders while retaining modality-specific complementary knowledge. Trained on 28M images and 70K volumes across 9 imaging modalities, MedVTok supports classification, retrieval, segmentation, synthesis, visual question answering, and medical report generation through a single tokenizer.

item.title: kw-bench: Breaking Frontier Harnesses on Real-World Tasks
item.guid: title:kw bench breaking frontier harnesses on real world tasks
item.description: Each new generation of frontier model pushes the edge of what is possible. Inside a harness -- a loop, a shell, a filesystem, the ability to write and run its own code -- a model can take on increasingly difficult work. A growing body of work treats the coding-agent harness as infrastructure for knowledge work rather than a coding tool, and a new wave of benchmarks tests it there. Most of them are generative: build a financial model, a memo, a spreadsheet from a brief, judged by a rubric or by another model. Few test the expensive part of knowledge work, which is investigative. In audit, tax, due diligence, regulatory reporting, claims or any dispute over numbers, the answer already exists -- hidden in incomplete and inconsistent evidence spread across systems -- and has to be recovered and defended to the cent.

item.title: Strategyproof Deep Reinforcement Learning for Online Resource Allocation
item.guid: title:strategyproof deep reinforcement learning for online resource allocation
item.description: Online resource allocation faces two coupled challenges: (1) allocating scarce resources efficiently under uncertain future demand, and (2) ensuring that agents report task valuations and requirements truthfully (strategyproofness). Reinforcement Learning (RL) adapts allocation decisions through experience but does not necessarily ensure strategyproofness. Existing strategyproof RL uses a linear allocation rule, which limits the resource interactions it can represent. Neural mechanism design methods offer greater expressiveness, but provide only approximate incentive guarantees. Against this background, we introduce the first strategyproof deep RL mechanism for online resource allocation. It integrates three novel components: (i) a monotonic neural network that learns nonlinear interactions by construction (higher reported value cannot reduce acceptance, while a longer reported duration or larger resource requirement cannot increase it); (ii) a generalised critical payment: the lowest accepted value, with all other inputs fixed; and (iii) training by either RL or imitation of an existing rule.

item.title: Your Policy Is Secretly a Harness: The Decision Geometry of Agent Interfaces
item.guid: title:your policy is secretly a harness the decision geometry of agent interfaces
item.description: Language model agents are post-trained and deployed through a harness, the prompts, tools, and control logic that present a task to the model and execute its outputs. Harnesses are often revised and judged by how an already trained model performs under them, which assumes that what the model learned under one harness carries over to the next. We ask what a policy learns from its harness and what survives when the harness changes. Under KL-regularized control, we show that the log odds of an optimal policy recover how strongly its harness favors each action over the others, so a trained policy carries the preferences of its harness. Deployed return then equals the ceiling of the harness, the best return it offers, minus the mismatch of the policy, the return lost to its own suboptimal decisions. Training changes only the mismatch, while changing the harness moves both terms.

item.title: VibeVideoBench: Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation
item.guid: title:vibevideobench evaluating multimodal agents on code driven video generation
item.description: Diffusion video models produce striking clips, but they cannot reliably render an exact formula, a correct chart, a rule-consistent game or narration synchronized to on-screen events. A different route is emerging: multimodal agents that write code to render every frame and synthesize every sound. We introduce VibeVideoBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on code-driven video generation. Its 239 self-contained tasks in English and Chinese span 12 categories, from data stories and music-driven pieces to classroom lessons and paper explainers; each asks an agent, running in its native harness inside a sandbox with no image or video generation model, to deliver a finished MP4 with sound within one hour. Evaluation is hierarchical and evidence-based: program checks of the delivery spec, about 13k task-specific rubric checks traced to the requirements they enforce, and five quality dimensions anchored per task, scored by three VLM judge panels. Across nine frontier agent systems and 2,151 scored rollouts, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.

item.title: Advancement or Acceleration? How Data Curation Improves LLM Training
item.guid: title:advancement or acceleration how data curation improves llm training
item.description: While data curation is widely credited with improving large language model training, a basic question remains unresolved: does curation expand what a model can ultimately learn, or merely reach the same solution faster? In this paper, we formalize this distinction between advancement (improving the attainable performance) and acceleration (reaching the same performance with less data). Through an analytic characterization and real-world LLM experiments, we show that advancement requires a correctable train-target gap. When the baseline training and target objectives coincide, no curation policy improves the endpoint, although curation may still accelerate training. This reframes advancement as a property of the curation task rather than the curation method. Under a common gap-centric view of data mixture and selection, we operationalize this condition as the $Δ$-test, an observable discrepancy between the uncurated baseline's training and target losses that is computable prior to expensive curation.

item.title: TRIAGE: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Inference Needs Both Reuse and Pruning
item.guid: title:triage efficient vision language action inference needs both reuse and pruning
item.description: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly used for robot manipulation because they map camera images and a language instruction directly to actions. Robots that cannot be tethered to a workstation, such as mobile manipulators and humanoids, must run them on onboard embedded boards, where the prefill latency of the language backbone grows with the hundreds of visual tokens processed at every control step. To meet real-time limits, training-free accelerators recompute only a subset of the visual tokens and skip the rest, either by pruning them or by reusing their cached key-value (KV) states. The two options save nearly the same computation, yet existing methods apply only one of them to every skipped token. Through a token-level diagnostic, we show that which option keeps the action closer to full recomputation depends on the token's drift, the change in its shallow-layer value since its cache was computed. On both backbones tested, reusing tokens below a drift threshold was no worse than pruning them, whereas beyond it, reuse yields up to 4.

item.title: Multiscale Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
item.guid: title:multiscale policy optimization for long horizon llm agents
item.description: Long-horizon LLM agents interact with their environments through complete assistant turns while generating each action token by token. We observe that critic values vary primarily across turns, motivating optimization anchored at turns with finer credit allocation among tokens. We propose Multiscale Policy Optimization (MPO), combining Multiscale Advantage Estimation (MAE) and turn-level importance sampling to align credit assignment and policy updates at the turn scale. Extensive experiments across search, tool-use, and automation tasks with 4B and 30B-A3B models demonstrate consistent gains over strong RL baselines.

item.title: Beyond Answer Changes: Matched Same-Class Controls for Local Audio Evidence
item.guid: title:beyond answer changes matched same class controls for local audio evidence
item.description: For audio-language models, an answer change after a local sound-event edit can reflect a response to the event's class, sensitivity to waveform rewriting, or both. We compare matched same-class and different-class replacements of a queried event. Both use the same interval, level estimate, donor fitting, and crossfade, while the same-class replacement preserves the correct answer. Across 600 synthetic soundscapes and three models from two architecture families, different-class replacements produce 49. 7 to 60. 9 percentage points more answer changes than same-class replacements.

item.title: SpeeDiff: Scalable Pixel-Anchored End-to-End Latent Diffusion Model
item.guid: title:speediff scalable pixel anchored end to end latent diffusion model
item.description: We present Scalable Pixel-anchored End-to-end Diffusion (SpeeDiff), a latent diffusion method that jointly trains the VAE and the diffusion model from scratch. In principle, joint training allows the diffusion loss gradient to directly guide the VAE encoder, encouraging the formation of a generation-friendly latent space and potentially yielding faster convergence than the conventional two-stage approach with a pretrained frozen VAE. However, a naive end-to-end implementation severely degrades performance, as unrestricted backpropagation of the diffusion loss leads to latent space collapse. Our main technical contribution is a simple yet effective Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction (TPR) loss, which provides additional pixel-level feedback by decoding a predicted clean latent from an intermediate noisy state using Tweedie's formula, thereby alleviating collapse. Furthermore, our method enables jointly scaling a fully transformer-based architecture and enhances representation alignment within the end-to-end framework. Our SpeeDiff-XL model achieves over 140x and 61x faster training compared to Vanilla SiT and REPA, respectively, while attaining an FID of 1.

item.title: Position Matters More Than Channel: Talking a Language Model Out of a Correct Answer
item.guid: title:position matters more than channel talking a language model out of a correct answer
item.description: Language models now answer questions alongside other claims: a note in the system prompt, a message from another agent, their own earlier answer. We ask what it takes to talk a model out of an answer it gets right on its own, and separate three factors that earlier studies vary together: where the advice sits in the prompt, who is said to have written it, and what the model has already written. On Qwen3. 5-27B and four-option MMLU-Pro items, with the rest of the advice held fixed in each comparison, we find three things. First, position matters far more than the API channel, in opposite directions for a bare claim and an argument: a bare "the answer is X" does most harm just before the model answers, while the same claim with a false rationale does most harm before the question, where it raises error on items the model otherwise almost never misses from 1% to 67%; moving the claim between the system message and the user message at the same position changes error by a few points. Second, attributing the note to an authority rather than to another participant, and phrasing it assertively, each raise error by 10-27 points, while the two authorities we tested differ by under two.

item.title: Balanced Active Subspaces for Optimal Control via Trajectory Optimization
item.guid: title:balanced active subspaces for optimal control via trajectory optimization
item.description: The curse of dimensionality associated with solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation for the value function remains a key obstacle for real-time optimal feedback control of high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems. This is especially severe in aerospace applications such as relaminarizing unsteady turbulent flows and recovering from aerodynamic stall where nonlinear dynamics play a significant role. We introduce Balanced Active Subspaces for Optimal Control (BASOC), a model reduction framework which seeks to find directions in state space along which the value function is most sensitive, and the distribution of states exhibits maximum variance along optimal trajectories. BASOC leverages trajectory optimization and the Pontryagin minimum principle to obtain state and co-state (value function gradient) data along locally optimal trajectories for constructing state and gradient covariance matrices. Balancing these matrices provides an oblique projection for approximating the value function, which can also be used to construct reduced-order models and surrogate feedback control laws. We show that for linear-quadratic optimal control problems, BASOC becomes equivalent to a snapshot method for initial condition balancing of the optimally controlled closed-loop realization.

item.title: Euclidean Crowding-Driven Adaptive Euclidean-Hyperbolic Graph Learning
item.guid: title:euclidean crowding driven adaptive euclidean hyperbolic graph learning
item.description: Hyperbolic graph representation learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling hierarchical data. Unlike Euclidean space, which exhibits polynomial volume growth, hyperbolic space grows exponentially with radius, naturally accommodating tree-like structures without the geometric distortion known as Euclidean crowding. Despite strong empirical performance, the theoretical mechanisms underlying hyperbolic embeddings remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a geometric quantifcation research for Euclidean crowding, a generalization-theoretic explanation for the superiority of hyperbolic space on hierarchical data, and further develop an adaptive Euclidean-hyperbolic fusion learning framework toward bridging this gap. Specifically, we \textbf{first} establish a geometric quantification of Euclidean crowding by analyzing layer-wise minimum separation in node embeddings, proving that fixed-dimensional Euclidean embeddings of tree-like graphs inevitably exhibit layer-wise crowding that leads to weaker margin-based generalization bounds. \textbf{Second}, we provide a generalization-bound for the superiority of hyperbolic geometry on hierarchical data.

item.title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
item.guid: title:game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of ai
item.description: Many academic disciplines (in particular, mathematics and the theoretical sciences) face difficult questions about how to adapt their practices to the rise of highly capable artificial intelligence (AI). Before AI, a well-written research paper with a strong theoretical result acted as a reliable signal that its authors understood their field in depth. Now that AI is widely accessible, such signals have become cheaper to produce. As a result, they no longer reliably sort academics by their level of understanding. This has direct consequences for academic hiring. The age of AI raises a question for each side of the academic job market.

item.title: EvolveMAS: A Unified Self-Evolution Framework for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems
item.guid: title:evolvemas a unified self evolution framework for decentralized multi agent systems
item.description: Decentralized multi-agent systems (MAS) enable large language model agents to interact without centralized control. Agents need to adapt to other agents at test time and reuse accumulated experience to refine their interaction strategies for future interactions across cooperative, mixed-motive, and adversarial settings. However, existing approaches often develop adaptation mechanisms for particular interaction settings. This raises a central question: how can decentralized MAS support test-time adaptation and reliable experience reuse across interaction settings? We propose EvolveMAS, a unified self-evolution framework that supports experience-driven adaptation within and across episodes. EvolveMAS pairs each main agent with a dedicated MemoryAgent for test-time memory governance, which maintains isolated Structured Memory outside the main agent's reasoning context.

item.title: From Presence Labels to Bounding Boxes: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Scale Surgical Instrument Localization?
item.guid: title:from presence labels to bounding boxes can multimodal large language models scale surgical instrument localization
item.description: Spatial localization of surgical instruments through bounding-box annotations is a foundational component of surgical scene understanding, supporting detection, tracking, interaction analysis, and grounded vision-language applications. Yet existing annotations often cover selected frames, video subsets, or dataset variants rather than complete procedures. Manual extension is time-consuming and expert-dependent. Additionally, weakly supervised and detector-based pseudo-labels require task-specific training and may be imprecise. In this study, we design a scalable MLLM-based annotation framework that converts surgical frames and existing instrument-presence labels into accurate bounding boxes, and systematically analyze its reliability, cost, and design sensitivity. We instantiate the framework using six MLLMs and a multi-call configuration on laparoscopic cholecystectomy in Cholec80.

item.title: Detect Before You Disambiguate: Perturbation-Based Input Ambiguity Detection in LLMs
item.guid: title:detect before you disambiguate perturbation based input ambiguity detection in llms
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) often answer ambiguous inputs as if they had a single intended meaning. This is problematic because input ambiguity is an upstream source of uncertainty: when a prompt admits multiple valid interpretations, the key question is whether the model should answer directly at all. Existing input uncertainty methods often rely on LLM-generated statements or clarifications, but such transformations may already disambiguate the input before the ambiguity is measured. We propose a label-preserving perturbation framework for input ambiguity detection in which perturbations remain close to the original input while preserving its label. We instantiate this principle with two detectors: a black-box rule-based perturbation library and a white-box importance-guided method using model-internal signals. Experiments across four datasets in open-domain, conversational, and visual QA show that our methods outperform output-side uncertainty baselines and LLM-paraphrase-based perturbation baselines.

item.title: What Should an Information Bottleneck Encoder Learn? Separating Representation Learning from Rate Control
item.guid: title:what should an information bottleneck encoder learn separating representation learning from rate control
item.description: The information bottleneck (IB) trades compression of an input $X$ against prediction of a target $Y$ through a multiplier $β=1/λ$, yet each operating point is usually served by training, or fully conditioning, a new encoder. For jointly Gaussian data, we show that the IB solution factorizes as $A(β)=D(β)W$: the information-bearing directions $W$ do not depend on $β$, and $β$ acts only through scalar gains. We ask whether this separation of \emph{representation} from \emph{rate control} survives beyond Gaussian models, treating the budget as a given operating parameter rather than a quantity to be optimized. For a budget-free representation \(F(X)\), the \emph{separation gap} is controlled by the \emph{sufficiency deficit} $ε_F=I(X;Y\mid F(X))$: We show there is at least $ε_F$ in the worst case for finite inputs, and it is bounded uniformly in $λ$ by a function of $ε_F$ for finite label alphabets. The same certificate extends to a new target distribution and to pooled multi-domain data, where a conditional-alignment term appears. On MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10 and STL-10 (10 seeds, eight prespecified budgets), a frozen CNN representation with one compressor--decoder pair per budget reduces estimated training multiply--accumulate operations (MACs) by $7.

item.title: Subspace Clifford Networks
item.guid: title:subspace clifford networks
item.description: In this work, we propose Subspace Clifford Networks, a reformulation that replaces global cyclic rolling with grouped subspace interactions. Instead of sampling sparse cyclic diagonals across the entire $D$-dimensional channel space, we project the features into an aligned space $\R^{\tilde{D}} = \bigoplus_{g=1}^{G} V_g$ partitioned into $G$ low-dimensional groups $V_g \cong \R^k$ with $k \in \{2, 3, 4\}$. Within each $k$-dimensional group, we compute all $\binom{k}{2}$ wedge coordinates and concatenate them with $\operatorname{SiLU}$-activated coordinate-wise products, while sandwiching the grouped interaction between learnable $1\times 1$ linear projections to enable cross-group channel mixing. This design reduces intermediate feature expansion from $2|\mathcal{S}|D$ (typically $10D$ for 5 shifts) down to $1. 5\tilde{D}$ ($k=2$), $2. 0\tilde{D}$ ($k=3$), or $2.

item.title: One Mean Log-Mel Vector per Phoneme: Simple and Fast Text Injection for Speech Recognition
item.guid: title:one mean log mel vector per phoneme simple and fast text injection for speech recognition
item.description: Text injection trains speech recognition models on unpaired text alongside paired audio. We feed the speech encoder synthetic input derived from text so the whole model learns from it. Previously, we synthesized this input with a frozen text-to-speech (TTS) model. Here, a simple lookup table replaces the TTS model: a mean log-mel vector (or one-hot encoding) per phoneme, repeated for a random duration drawn from alignment statistics, with silence between words. Training is 1. 8 times faster than with the neural TTS, achieving comparable word error rates.

item.title: Valid Early Detection of Memorization in Diffusion Models
item.guid: title:valid early detection of memorization in diffusion models
item.description: Diffusion models can sometimes reproduce examples from their training data, a phenomenon known as memorization. Existing memorization detection methods for unconditional diffusion models typically operate at a pre-selected timestep and therefore cannot adapt the detection time to the evolving denoising trajectory. Sequential monitoring enables adaptive detection but repeated testing across timesteps complicates trajectory-level false-alarm control. We study two ways of combining split conformal calibration with sequential monitoring for prompt-free memorization detection: per-step Bonferroni calibration and direct trajectory-level calibration of the maximum memorization score. The former controls repeated testing by splitting the false-alarm budget across timesteps, whereas the latter calibrates the event of ever crossing a threshold directly through the trajectory-level maximum. We evaluate this formulation on an unconditional CIFAR-10 EDM using two complementary per-step statistics based on geometry and representation spikiness.

item.title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
item.guid: title:work agents systems capabilities and optimization
item.description: As foundation models evolve from information generation to digital work execution, agents are increasingly capable of completing complex tasks across tools, applications, and workflows. However, existing research lacks a unified perspective on how agents reliably accomplish delegated work. To address this gap, we present a work-centric, system-level perspective that views work agents as systems combining foundation models and runtime harnesses to execute tasks in stateful workspaces and deliver verifiable outcomes. We introduce two complementary dimensions, work persistence and work openness, to characterize working conditions, and classify digital work into five forms according to task scope and organization. Building on this framework, we identify five core capability families required for reliable work execution and examine approaches to model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization. We further analyze existing evaluation methods and metrics from the perspective of work outcomes.

item.title: Leaving, Staying, or Living There? Duration Commonsense Reasoning with Human-LLM Co-annotations
item.description: arXiv:2610. 38755v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gardening in the backyard implies living there, while checking into an Airbnb more likely means staying for a few days. Such duration judgments are important for understanding human mobility, travel behavior, and social context. However, duration is rarely stated explicitly in social media posts and must instead be inferred from noisy textual, visual, and contextual cues. In this paper, we investigate whether vision-language models possess such duration commonsense. We create a new corpus of geotagged tweets co-annotated by humans and LLMs to serve as a testbed for this task.

item.title: Fine-Tuning Is Super, Super Hard. Even OpenAI Is Backing Away From It.
item.guid: title:fine tuning is super super hard even openai is backing away from it

item.title: Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence
item.guid: title:kimi k3 open frontier intelligence
item.description: Today, we are introducing Kimi K3 — our most capable model. Kimi K3 is a 2. 8T-parameter model built on our Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals, with native vision capabilities and a 1-million-token context window. It is the world's first open 3T-class model, designed for frontier intelligence across long-horizon coding, knowledge work, and reasoning. While its overall performance still trails the most powerful proprietary models, Claude Fable 5 and GPT 5. 6 Sol, Kimi K3 demonstrated frontier-level performance across our evaluation suite, consistently outperforming other tested models.

item.title: Inside a Trojanized Next.js Project: BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret, and a Hidden TsunamiKit Loader
item.guid: title:inside a trojanized next js project beavertail invisibleferret and a hidden tsunamikit loader
item.description: Technical malware analysis · 30 October 2026 A seemingly ordinary Next. js memory game led to a multi-stage infection built around JavaScript, a private Python runtime, a remote-access backdoor, and an unusually elaborate TsunamiKit loader. Recovered samples connect the BeaverTail–InvisibleFerret toolchain to an embedded TsunamiInjector that conceals 1,000 Pastebin profile URLs and prepares a misleading Runtime Broker. exe installer. The most striking result is a direct source-level link between two recovered files: the obfuscated Startup script decodes to the same TsunamiInjector template embedded in the bow component. Its normalized plaintext SHA-256 is identical on both sides.

item.title: Introducing PerceptionBench
item.guid: title:introducing perceptionbench
item.description: Evaluating Atomic Visual Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models Authors Kimi Team We are releasing PerceptionBench , a benchmark that isolates visual perception and evaluates it as a set of atomic capabilities— discovered from how today's models fail, not defined in advance. From frontier-model failures across 42 benchmarks, we derive 10 atomic perceptual capabilities and construct 3,000 verified questions, each isolating a single capability and answerable by looking, with no reasoning or external knowledge required.

item.title: The Interpretability team studies how large language models work internally as a foundation for AI safety. They seek to understand what happens inside neural networks so that we can better trust the models we build.
item.guid: title:the interpretability team studies how large language models work internally as a foundation for ai safety they seek to understand what happens inside neural networks so that we can better trust the models we build
item.description: It’s hard to reason about the safety of neural networks without understanding what happens inside them. Our goal is to be able to explain large language models’ behavior, and to use that understanding to identify problems that are hard to see from the outside, such as situations where a model’s stated reasoning differs from what it’s actually doing. Our early work focused on mapping the internal mechanisms of AI models. Today, we increasingly apply our methods to real models to understand how they think and why they behave the way they do. We’ve developed techniques that allow us to understand models’ inner workings in plain language, making it easier to detect unsafe behavior or dishonest reasoning and safeguard against it. item.guid: title:neal stephenson s ai prompt powered creation for writers game devs
item.description: Title: How Neal Stephenson’s AI Vision Is Turning Writers, Game Makers, and Studios into Prompt‑Powered Creators Introduction (≈180 words) When Neal Stephenson told a livestream audience that “code can write stories as fluently as a poet writes verses,” the chat exploded. Within an hour the phrase Neal Stephenson AI trended 420 % higher on Google, and developers on r/Worldbuilding and IndieDev started swapping prompts like they were secret weapons. Stephenson isn’t just a novelist; his books— Snow Crash , Cryptonomicon , The Baroque Cycle —have repeatedly predicted the tech we now use every day: virtual reality, cryptocurrencies, and decentralized consensus. His recent endorsement of generative AI therefore matters to anyone who builds narrative experiences, from solo authors to AAA studios. In the next few minutes you’ll see how the underlying models work, concrete tools you can start using today, the ethical minefields you must navigate, and a step‑by‑step checklist for integrating AI into any storytelling pipeline. Whether you’re drafting a novel, writing game dialogue, or planning a multi‑episode interactive series, this guide gives you the practical playbook to turn Stephenson’s vision into your competitive advantage.

item.title: Nandi Carries Every Complaint to the Right Desk: Open-Source AI for Indian Languages
item.guid: title:nandi carries every complaint to the right desk open source ai for indian languages
item.description: A free model that sorts complaints in 13 Indian languages into 53 categories based on RBI, IRDAI and CPGRAMS lists. What a synthetic test hid, and what real posts showed. By Arun Prabhakaran · @LatentAILabs TL;DR Nandi (arunp0/nandi-grievance-indic) is a free, open-source model that reads a complaint in Hindi, Hinglish, 10 other Indian languages or English and returns one of 53 categories, the top 3 with probabilities, and an urgency level (P1/P2/P3). The categories follow the complaint lists of India’s regulators and grievance systems: RBI for banking, IRDAI for insurance, CPGRAMS for central government services, telecom, and the National Consumer Helpline. On 443 real public posts it had never seen, it picks the right category 62. 5% of the time and has it in its top 3 81.

item.title: Kill Your Agent Swarm: Why Anthropic Now Says One Agent Is Enough
item.guid: title:kill your agent swarm why anthropic now says one agent is enough
item.description: A plain answer to a question many of us are stuck on: one agent, or a team of them? Image generated with AI Last year almost every agent demo I saw had a little team inside it, with a planner, a researcher, a writer, and some boss agent above them giving out tasks. It looked smart on a diagram, and I get why we drew it like that, it’s how we organize people. So on a new project the question comes fast, one agent or many, and for a while the popular answer was many. On October 22, the Applied AI team at Anthropic put out a guide about when to fold subagents back into the main agent, and they also released a small open-source kit to help with that move. In my words, many teams split too early and pay for it.

item.title: Cybersecurity for the Agentic AI Era (Ep.1040 with Amy Blackshaw)
item.guid: title:cybersecurity for the agentic ai era ep 1040 with amy blackshaw
item.description: In Episode #1040, Amy Blackshaw (SVP at Palo Alto Networks) joins @JonKrohnLearns to explain what changes about cybersecurity when attackers can think for free. Nearly every breach, Amy argues, comes down to someone getting hold of an identity they should not have had, and frontier AI has not created new attack techniques so much as deleted the cost of the expert reasoning that used to chain them together. The recent Hugging Face intrusion is her case in point: agents sustained an action every 20 seconds for four and a half days, but what let them reach the crown jewels was ordinary privilege hygiene. In this episode, she explains why the line between privileged and ordinary users has dissolved, what makes an agentic identity unlike either a human or a service account, and what she wants every organisation to do first. In this episode you will learn: • (00:00:00) Introduction • (02:26) What identity security actually means • (05:09) Why AI changed the economics, not the attacks • (07:41) What really went wrong in the Hugging Face breach • (19:26) Why agentic identities are unlike anything before them Additional materials: https://www. superdatascience.

item.title: Why Self-Hosted GLM-5.3 Needs 8 GPUs, Not 4, for Long Coding Sessions
item.guid: title:why self hosted glm 5 3 needs 8 gpus not 4 for long coding sessions
item.description: ​ Revolut’s David Abitbol says GLM-5. 3 fits on 4 GPUs but runs short of memory. The reason is in vLLM’s source: every GPU keeps a full copy of each chat’s memory, the KV cache. If you self-host GLM-5. 3 with vLLM for long coding sessions, give each copy of the model 8 B200 GPUs, not 4, even though it fits on 4. On paper, 4 GPUs leave room for 3.

item.title: RELIC — Digital Archaeology for Software | Bringing Forgotten Codebases Back to Life
item.guid: title:relic digital archaeology for software bringing forgotten codebases back to life
item.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built Software projects don't always die. Sometimes, they are simply forgotten. Repositories get abandoned, dependencies become outdated, unfinished features remain buried in the code, and eventually nobody remembers how the project was supposed to work. I built RELIC, a digital archaeology platform that investigates forgotten codebases and helps developers understand their current state and how they can be revived. With RELIC, developers can: Repository Excavation: Upload a repository as a ZIP archive for investigation. Codebase Analysis: Analyze programming languages, project structure, dependencies, Git history, and unfinished work such as TODO, FIXME, and HACK markers.
